newsitem.title: UK: UK monetary reforms to clean out political meddling.
newsitem.headline: UK monetary reforms to clean out political meddling.

text.p: New powers granting the Bank of England control over interest rates have, in a single step, purged the monetary policy process of political meddling and greatly increased the chances of lower inflation in Britain.

The new Labour government stunned financial markets on Tuesday when it announced the central bank would have operational independence to set interest rates and fleshed out plans for a new monetary policy committee which will hold executive power.
"These changes...amount to the most radical internal reform of the Bank of England since is was established in 1694, over 300 years ago," the new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said.

"We must remove the suspicion that short-term party-political considerations are influencing the setting of interest rates," he told his first news conference since Labour's landslide election victory on May 1.
A new monetary policy committee will be set up within the Bank to decide the level of rates each month with no government representatives among its nine members.
Brown further endeared himself to the central bank by raising interest rates by a quarter point to prevent inflation getting out of hand.
Economists in London's financial square mile gave the news a spirited reception, saying they were confident the new structure would help inflation to fall further.

"Central bank independence is the single most fashionable thing among economists at the moment so Gordon Brown is doing the right thing by most commentators," said David Mackie, U.K. economist at JP Morgan.
He said the new structure would probably mean lower inflation in the future, but also higher interest rates.
The Bank has frequently opposed government decisions to cut interest rates -- most recently in June 1996 -- and has been in favour of higher rates since last December.
Mackie said even if the four external appointees to the Bank's nine-strong monetary policy committee were soft on inflation to start with, their dovish tendencies would not last long.

"Even if the outsiders appointed to the monetary policy committee start off dovish they will be in close contact with (Governor) Eddie George day-to-day and will be briefed by Bank economists, so they are likely to rapidly become insiders and inflation hawks."
Many economists were stunned by the speed with which the new chancellor (finance minister) had acted, and his early departure from Labour's line before the election.

"Labour said during the campaign that it was in favour of more independence but the Bank needed a longer track record, so this is really quite a shock," said Michael Dicks, U.K. economist at Lehman Brothers.
"It is very much related to the European question, the closer ties with Europe and the single European currency."
The legislation will bring Britain closer to meeting the criteria laid down by the Maastricht Treaty for European economic and monetary union (EMU), but it falls short of fully satisfying the terms.

"This is a building block, a launch pad. But this is not enough. The Bank has to be made entirely independent and the government has retained its right to issue instructions," said Graham Bishop, adviser on European financial affairs at Salomon Brothers.
Bishop, a leading expert on EMU and adviser to the Treasury Committee in the House of Commons, told Reuters that subsequent changes to satisfy Maastricht may only have to be minimal.
"It may be that the legislation will only need a short clause to be added -- in which the government gives up its residual right to instruct -- in order to satisfy Maastricht," he said.
"This will help relations in Europe. It will be very well received although there may be a little disappointment that the U.K. hasn't moved to full independence."
But the new legislation will bring to an end the high profile monthly monetary meetings, dubbed the "Ken and Eddie show" under Kenneth Clarke's reign as chancellor.
"That's a bit sad, but the new arrangements will retain the openness that characterised those meetings with minutes and the vote on rates both published," said Mackie.
